If you are going to have a homestead, at some point, you may need a Come Along. My wife and I bought a small farm last year. The Come Along can be used for a lot of things like pulling a truck/car/atv out of the mud, tightening up fence lines and wenching up engines. London is set for another day of anti-austerity marches - what's your view on cutting our public services?

As an American - I never liked the shift of local to centralized funding. Too strong of a central government. I think there should be competition in ideas and we should feed the good ones and move away from the ideas that fail.

"In the old days... and smaller towns.." The Church and such idealistic organizations would educate people on caring for their neighbor. Get to know your neighbor, love your neighbor, etc. If they were starving, give them some food. If they had a death in the family, help with the children.

Well, now we get taxed, mail money to a central processing office, then the benefits come in a generic form of payment. Our Public Services have become dehumanized by geography shifting to a central office - and to a systemic approach. Cue Terry Gilliam's film Brazil from 1985.

Exaggerating a bit: There is no Love and Compassion in such a system. The neighbors do not find out that the guy next door is poor and needs help. And one day they find out that he drank himself to death or suicide due to depression.

People are protesting together, but I'm not really sure that's more than another quick-fix solution - in an attempt to not deal with the issues all around them. "Have the Government fix our marriages, our conflicts, and how to take care of the difficult alcoholic next door!"

Canada used to be a very socialized country, much like the United Kingdom is today, or perhaps Sweden, but then it was found to be unsustainable. When your economy is not generating enough money you cannot maintain generous benefits, or other programs that do not directly contribute to your country's wealth. They can protest all they want, but it has to happen.

While a country in which the entire populace can sustain themselves would be ideal, it will never be the case, and here's why:

Firstly, we'd need to make sure that there are an equal number (or greater) of jobs than unemployed people. If we have less vacant jobs than unemployed people, there will be people without jobs, and therefore without money. This doesn't even account for the amount of these jobs that require specialist skills. If McDonald's wanted to, they could replace their entire front-counter staff with self-service machines that would do a better job in a fraction of the time. I've worked in McDonald's, and I can attest that a customer can take their own order better than I ever could, because I'm a human and I mishear people/forget things.

Secondly, to tie in with the first point, the people who are surplus to our employment requirements would not have any means of sustaining themselves if the country continues to move to a self-sustaining state (if we continue to make cuts to benefits and such). Do you expect these people to just roll over and die? Of course they aren't going to. If I didn't have a job and needed money, there is a long line of things I would do before I gave up and starved to death, and eventually you slip from legitimate means to illegitimate means.

Imagine you have an extensive criminal record and nobody will employ you, are you going to starve to death or are you going to return to crime to answer your problems? Most people in this situation would choose the latter. When these people eventually get caught (after who knows how many robberies, drug deals, etc), we are then paying to imprison them (just take a look at the costs involved).

While I disagree with paying for others to do nothing all day, I'd take that over being mugged by someone who sees no other options.
It's funny, it's such simple logic that it's not really up for political debate, it just is what it is.
Cut them back to the bare bones.

There are obviously plenty of areas where money is wasted in public services (like buying brand-name medicines on the NHS) but I'm not sure that the same level of service can be provided with the scale of these upcoming cuts. There are several areas where it makes sense to increase funding like science/technology as they give a good long-term return on investment, and the NHS, because it's facing increased pressure from changing demographics. However, I'm all for reducing waste where it's an easy win.

Also the whole idea that we need a budget surplus right now is crazy. Our borrowing rates are basically zero, we should be taking that money and investing it in our terrible transport infrastructure to boost growth.
